---
title: "Retiring the Question"
abstract: |
  On a standard view, inquiry is an interrogative attitude toward a question, and an inquiry succeeds when its question is answered. Norms of inquiry are accordingly stated over questions: do not inquire into a question with a false presupposition; do not inquire while believing a complete answer. I argue that many successful inquiries end by retiring their question, because it presupposed something false or because answering it would not relieve what prompted it. The defect can usually be found only by pursuing the question. So a norm forbidding inquiry into defective questions is either idle, because it bites only once the defect is known, or it blocks the practice through which defects are found. The success of an inquiry cannot be read off its question. I propose that inquiries are individuated by problems, and that an inquiry succeeds when what it found relieves the problem, whether by answering, dissolving or replacing the question.

# The question-first picture {#sec-picture}

Inquiry is now commonly understood as an interrogative attitude toward a question: wondering, being curious, having the question on one's agenda. The attitude is goal-directed: "in inquiring into some question we aim to resolve or answer the question" [@friedman2017, 307]. When an inquiry goes well, "we settle some matter that previously was or felt unsettled to us" [@friedman2019, sec. 1]. If that is the structure of inquiry, norms of inquiry are naturally stated over questions, and they are:

- *Don't Believe and Inquire*: one ought not inquire into Q at a time and also believe a complete answer to Q at that time [@friedman2019].
- *No Defective Questions*: one ought to inquire into an unconditional question Q only if Q has a true, complete and direct answer. A question is defective when one of its presuppositions is false [@willardkyle2023]. Willard-Kyle's stronger *Knowledge Norm for Inquiry* requires that one know Q has such an answer.
- *Sound Question Norm*: it is irrational to wonder Q while one's knowledge does not entail all of Q's presuppositions [@whitcombmillson2023].
- *No False Presuppositions*: one should not inquire into questions that rely on false presuppositions. Rosa's reason is that "In inquiring into Q, one aims at finding the true answer to Q," and there is none to find [@rosa2025].

These norms differ in strength and in what they are norms of. They share an assumption: what counts as an inquiry succeeding is fixed by its question. Call this the question-first picture. The inquirer has a question, the question has a space of answers, and the inquiry succeeds if she lands in the right part of it.

I think this is wrong, and that the way it is wrong shows that the norms built on it are idle or harmful. Three claims. First, many paradigm successful inquiries end by retiring their question: the presupposition fails, or answering would not help. Second, the defect that leads to retirement can usually be discovered only by inquiring into the question. So a norm that forbids inquiry into defective questions either bites only after the defect is known, in which case it is idle, or it applies to agents who do not yet know, in which case it forbids the practice by which defects are found. Third, and independently of the second, the success of an inquiry is not determined by its question. It is determined by the problem the question serves, and an inquiry succeeds when what it found relieves that problem, which may be by answering the question, by dissolving it, or by replacing it with another.

The sections that follow give cases (@sec-cases), the argument from discovery (@sec-discovery), the argument that success cannot be read off the question (@sec-success), the positive view (@sec-problems), a test of whether the disagreement is verbal (@sec-verbal), and the closest prior work (@sec-prior).

# Inquiries that end by retiring their questions {#sec-cases}

**The shortfall.** Ines manages a café. The Friday till is £200 short. She asks: which of my three cashiers took it? She watches the till, reconciles receipts and talks to staff. (The case is constructed; it is built to isolate one feature.)

In version A she finds that a cash payment to a supplier was entered twice on Thursday's sheet. The till was never short. In version B the till really is short and the receipts reconcile. The security camera shows the supplier's driver lifting cash from the open drawer while the cashier was in the stock room.

In both versions the question "Which cashier took the £200?" has a false presupposition, and in both Ines learns that no cashier took it. In A she may stop. Her trouble has gone, she knows why, and nothing is left to settle. In B she may not stop. She has learned something, perhaps something important, but her trouble is intact: money is gone and she does not know how or whom to pursue. It would be a mistake, not a rest, to treat the matter as closed. Only when she asks a new question, about the driver, and settles it, has she done what she set out to do.

Two points. Her inquiry in A is a success even though the question she asked was never directly answered. And whether the same discovery, that no cashier took it, ends an inquiry or merely redirects it does not depend on the question or its defect, which are identical across A and B. I return to this pair in @sec-success.

**The ether.** The history is richer than a case can carry, so I take only what the primary texts support. Michelson and Morley set out to measure the relative motion of the earth and the luminiferous ether. They concluded that "the relative velocity of the earth and the ether is probably less than one sixth the earth's orbital velocity," that "if there be any relative motion between the earth and the luminiferous ether, it must be small," and that it was small enough to refute Fresnel's explanation of aberration [@michelson1887]. Eighteen years later Einstein opens his paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies with "the unsuccessful attempts to discover any motion of the earth relatively to the 'light medium,'" and announces that "the introduction of a 'luminiferous ether' will prove to be superfluous" [@einstein1905]. I use this as follows. An extended inquiry, carried on by many people, began with a question about how fast the earth moves through a medium. For those who followed Einstein, it ended in a theory on which that question is not raised, because there is no distinguished state of rest against which to measure. Einstein says "superfluous" rather than "false," and I do not claim his wording is a denial of a presupposition. I claim that the inquiry that began with the velocity question is, by any standard physicists apply, among the most successful in the history of physics, and that it ended by retiring that question. The 1887 authors did not know the question was defective, and could hardly have found out without doing something very like what they did.

**Two ways to retire a question.** The shortfall and the ether are cases of presupposition failure. A question can also be retired while perfectly sound. Suppose a patient with chronic pain asks which of twelve candidate drugs reduces her pain most. There is such a drug, so the question is sound. Early on she learns that the pain comes from how she sits at her desk. The question is no longer worth answering, and she is right to drop it. The inquiry has succeeded and the question has been retired without any defect. Soundness is neither necessary nor sufficient for the question to be the thing to go on asking.

# The argument from discovery {#sec-discovery}

Call a question *defective* if one of its presuppositions is false, as Willard-Kyle does. The argument has three steps.

**Step one: defects are typically found by pursuing the question.** There are cheap defects, knowable without inquiring: that two plus two is five, that the sun sets in the east, that there is a barber who shaves all and only those who do not shave themselves. Willard-Kyle's five examples of defective questions are all of this kind [@willardkyle2023, sec. 3.1]. But the defects that matter to the practice of inquiry are of the other kind, where the evidence about whether the presupposition holds is not available until one tries to answer. The evidence bearing on whether there is a velocity of the earth through the ether is what you get by trying to determine it. The evidence that no cashier took the money is what you get by checking what each cashier did. This is not a coincidence. A presupposition of an empirical question is a claim about the subject matter of the question, and the evidence that bears on it is typically the evidence that bears on the answer.

**Step two: the norms are either idle or forbid the practice.** Take the versions that require knowledge of the defect. Friedman observes that once one realizes a question has a false presupposition, "further inquiry into Q would be irrational or otherwise epistemically inappropriate" [@friedman2017, 315--316]. Willard-Kyle's weaker *No Known-to-be-Defective Questions* is similar. These are plausible, and idle. They apply after the defect is known, which on every view is when the inquiry into Q is over. They say nothing about the inquiry through which the defect was found, and nothing about whether that inquiry was well conducted.

Now take the versions that apply to the agent who does not know. *No Defective Questions* in its fact-relative form says Ines should not inquire into the question in either version, since it is defective in both. The epistemic forms, the Knowledge Norm and the Sound Question Norm, say it more cleanly: she does not know the presuppositions, so she should not wonder. If the norms are prescriptive for agents in Ines's position, and Ines had followed them, she would never have found out about the driver, or the double entry. Applied to the community, they would have stopped the measurements that led to the end of the ether question. A norm whose purpose is to spare inquirers from chasing what is not there would have preserved the confusion.

**Replies, and why they do not rescue the norms.**

*The excuse reply.* Willard-Kyle himself writes that "Mistakes can be engines of discovery," and that when we discover we have inquired into a defective question, "we stop asking it, revising our question if necessary." Reflective agents, he adds, "are prepared to learn from their failed inquiries as well as their successful ones" [@willardkyle2023, sec. 6]. So the norm is violated, excusably, and something is learned. I accept the last part. But this reply already classifies Ines's inquiry in A as a failed inquiry. I take that up in @sec-verbal. Notice for now that "excusable violation" does not settle what we are to say of her at the moment she completes the inquiry and is right to stop.

*The pro tanto reply.* Rosa raises the objection that inquiry into a defective question can pay off: "my inquiry into what the largest prime number is... leads me to learn that there isn't such a number to begin with" [@rosa2025]. His answer is that the norms are not all-things-considered. As far as the goal constitutive of inquiring is concerned, which is finding the true answer to Q, one should not inquire into Q, though other goals may favor it [@rosa2025]. This depends on what the constitutive goal is. Rosa's inquirer, having learned that there is no largest prime, is not left with an unmet aim. She stops, rationally, with no sense that what she was trying to settle is still open. If the goal "find the true answer to Q" can be frustrated while the agent rationally stops with no residue of unsettledness, it is not the goal she was pursuing. Compare an inquirer who fails to find the answer to a sound question: the unsettledness remains, and so does her reason to continue. Rosa can say that she aimed at the answer, failed, and is pleased about something else. But the something else is what she learned, and the account then owes an explanation of why the failed inquiry leaves her better placed than a successful one would have. By Friedman's own gloss, the mark of success is that a matter which was unsettled is now settled, and the largest-prime inquirer meets it.

*The evaluative reply.* Palmira separates evaluative norms, which set the standard of goodness for activities of inquiry qua inquiry, from prescriptive norms, which govern what is permitted. She endorses an evaluative norm that there is something good about inquiry that can deliver knowledgeable answers to the questions under investigation, and something bad about inquiry that cannot [@palmira2025]. This is the best form of the view I oppose, because it grants permissibility to inquirers who are uncertain and still ties the quality of the inquiry to answers to its question. My argument is that this evaluative norm, read as being about direct answers, is false of Ines in A and of the largest-prime inquirer. Their inquiries could not deliver knowledgeable direct answers to the questions they began with, and they are not bad inquiries. They did what inquiry is for.

*Reformulation.* One might say Ines should have inquired into a different question: whether any cashier took it. That question has a true answer in both versions. This is the move Falbo describes as "questions with easy entailments," and she objects that it is ad hoc and psychologically unrealistic, and that why-questions have no easy-entailment variants [@falbo2024]. I add a dilemma. Ines's activity is the same whether we describe it as pursuing "which cashier?" or "whether any cashier?" Her observations, reconciliations and interviews do not come in two versions. If reformulation is allowed as a mere redescription of the same activity, the norm constrains only the labels we attach, and every inquiry into a defective question conforms to the norm under some label. If it is not allowed, the norm forbids the activity. Either way it does no work.

The same goes for *conditional questions*. Willard-Kyle restricts his norms to unconditional questions and tentatively suggests that conditional questions are hedges that remove the assumption that the asker knows the antecedent; he sets a full treatment aside [@willardkyle2023, note 8]. Suppose Ines asks "If a cashier took it, which?" Whether the falsity of the antecedent counts as an answer, a dissolution or a vacuity, it is the same in A and in B, and the pair still differs in whether she may stop. So the conditional form, even if it licenses the inquiry, does not tell us when the inquiry is over.

# Success is not fixed by the question {#sec-success}

The argument from discovery shows the norms cannot be right as prescriptive norms for uncertain agents. The deeper issue is the question-first assumption underneath them: that an inquiry's success is fixed by its question. The shortfall pair is a counterexample to that assumption, and there are three ways to resist it.

**Extend the answer space.** The most natural reply is that denying a presupposition is itself a kind of answer. To deny a presupposition of a question is to give a corrective answer, and the Stanford Encyclopedia says that "most theorists join Belnap and Steel in not counting corrective answers as direct answers" [@cross-roelofsen-sep; @belnapsteel1976]. Willard-Kyle is ecumenical about it, and words his Knowledge Norm so that readers may take "direct" or leave it [@willardkyle2023, sec. 2.2]. So one could say: success is resolution in an enlarged answer space that includes corrective answers. Ines gets one in both versions. She succeeds in both.

This fails for two reasons. First, in the shortfall pair she receives the same corrective answer, "no cashier took it," in A and in B, and A is complete while B is not. An enlarged answer space that counts the corrective answer as a resolution calls B a success, wrongly, and one that does not calls A a failure, also wrongly. There is nothing in the question and the answer, taken together, that separates the two. The difference lies elsewhere: in A the discovery relieves what prompted the question, and in B it does not.

Second, replacing a question by another is not a case of denying a presupposition. When Ines moves in B from "which cashier?" to "which person took the money from the open drawer?" she gives a corrective answer to the first and adopts the second. The answers to the second are not corrective answers to the first, nor boolean combinations of its answers. The question about the driver has a cell for each person who might have been responsible. "Which cashier?" has a cell for each cashier, and the extra cell for "none" says nothing about who instead. In the ether case the contrast is greater. The answers to the questions the new theory answers, about how space and time measurements in different frames must be related, are not unions of cells of "how fast is the earth moving through the ether?" Whatever extension of the old answer space we choose, the new question's answers are not in it. An inquiry that runs from Q to Q′ is not a single resolution of Q in any answer space for Q.

**A chain of questions.** A second reply: success is the answering of the last question in a chain, where each question replaces the previous one when the previous is found defective. Ines in A asks "what explains the apparent shortfall?" next, and answers it. This is closer to the truth, but it needs a relation that makes a sequence of questions into one inquiry. Why is "who took it?" a continuation of Ines's inquiry and not a new one she might have started anyway? It is not just that she asks them in sequence. The answer is that the new question is adopted because the old one failed to relieve the trouble that prompted it, and is expected to. That relation is not between questions. It is between the questions and something that persists through the change, which is the thing I shall call the problem. A chain view that admits such a relation is my view under another name. A chain view that does not has no way to say that B is unfinished while A is finished.

**The real question was always bigger.** A third reply: Ines's real question was never "which cashier?" but "what happened to the money?" That is a sound question and her inquiry succeeds if and only if it is answered. In A, she answers it; in B she is still working on it. I take this to be correct as a description of the cases and as a concession. If the question that fixes success is always the one the inquirer was really trying to settle, then success is fixed by what she was trying to settle, which is the problem, and the question she asked aloud is not what determines it. The norms in the literature are not stated over that bigger question. They are stated over the question the inquirer is asking, with its presuppositions, partition and answers, and if it is the question asked that is defective, the norm applies to that one. The bigger question has several marks of what I mean by a problem and not of a question in the sense those norms need. It often cannot be stated at the start with a determinate set of answers. Ines can say "what happened to the money?", but that is a placeholder for whatever turns out to explain the loss, and its answers cannot be listed in advance. In the ether case, the question the new theory answers is stated with concepts, such as a relativized notion of simultaneity, that the inquiry itself produced. A question whose answer space exists only after the inquiry has done its work cannot be what fixed the inquiry's success in advance.

So each repair either fails or turns into a view on which something other than the single asked question fixes success. @sec-problems states that view.

# Problems, not questions {#sec-problems}

**Problems.** People ask questions in order to do something about something: to remove a puzzle, restore an equilibrium, make a decision, explain an anomaly. Call the thing to be done about something a *problem*. It consists of a *trouble*, which is a state of the inquirer that she wants to be rid of (an unexplained datum, a conflict among her commitments, a decision that cannot be made on what she knows), and a *standard of relief*, which says what would count as being rid of it. A question is a proposal about how to meet the standard: if I knew the answer to Q, the trouble would go. At any stage of an inquiry the inquirer has a *current question* that she is pursuing as the best available means to relieve the trouble. When the current question turns out to be defective, or no longer a good means, she changes it and carries on.

**Individuation.** An inquiry is a stretch of activity directed at relieving a given problem. Stages under different questions Q and Q′ belong to one inquiry when two conditions hold: Q′ was adopted in light of what was found while pursuing Q, and it was adopted as a better means to relieve the very trouble Q was adopted to relieve. A test for the second condition: if she learned the answer to Q′, would she count the trouble as relieved, and if she had learned an answer to Q alone, would she have counted it as unrelieved? For Ines in B, yes to both. She would regard the matter as closed if she knew who took the money from the drawer, and not if she knew only that it was not a cashier.

**Success.** An inquiry succeeds when it ends in a state in which (i) the trouble is relieved by the standard of relief the inquirer began with, or by a revision of that standard that she can defend on the basis of what the inquiry found; (ii) the relief is due to what the inquiry found, not to luck or to the passage of time; and (iii) her state at the end is epistemically good: she knows, or understands, what the relief rests on. She is then rationally able to stop. If instead she can see that the trouble remains, she cannot rationally treat the inquiry as finished (A is complete; B is not). If it remains and she stops anyway, she has abandoned it.

*Answering as a special case.* When the trouble is the open question itself, which is the case the question-first picture has in mind, relief just is knowing the answer. The view agrees with the standard view where the standard view is plausible. It differs in cases where the question is not the trouble but a proposal about how to meet it.

*Abandonment, and moving the goalposts.* The obvious danger is that any inquirer who fails to answer her question can claim success by redescribing what she wanted. Three constraints guard against this. The trouble must be fixed by her reasons for beginning, which are independent of how things turn out. The relief must come from what the inquiry found: if she says "what I wanted all along was the experience," and nothing she found bears on the original trouble, she has abandoned the inquiry. And the end state must be epistemically good: someone who mistakenly believes the presupposition false and stops has not succeeded, whatever her feelings.

*Where the existing norms go.* The picture does not discard the norms. Don't Believe and Inquire is a norm about how a believed answer relates to the current question, and it stands. Hubacher Haerle's *Success Norm* says it is irrational to inquire when one cannot rationally believe that one will succeed [@hubacherhaerle2025]. With success understood as relief of the problem, an inquirer who is uncertain whether her question is sound can rationally expect to succeed, since she can expect that either an answer or the discovery of a defect will relieve the problem, and the norm does not forbid her to begin. What goes is the claim that soundness of the current question is a condition on inquiring.

**Relation to the idea of "settling."** Friedman's gloss on success is stated in terms of settling a matter, but her norms are stated in terms of answering a question. I take the gloss and reject the question as the unit. What is settled is the problem, and the question is a means.

# Is the dispute verbal? {#sec-verbal}

A reader may think the whole disagreement is about whether to call the shortfall inquiry in A "successful" or "failed in an informative way." Willard-Kyle's phrase is "failed inquiries," and he notes that reflective agents learn from these as well as from successful ones [@willardkyle2023, sec. 6]. I think the disagreement is substantive. Four places show it.

**First, the stopping verdict.** On the question-first picture, discovering that Q is defective makes further inquiry into Q inappropriate [@friedman2017, 315--316], and Willard-Kyle's advice is that we stop asking it, "revising our question if necessary." Ines in B stops asking the cashier question. The words "if necessary" carry the weight. When is revising necessary? Nothing in the question or its defect says, and the pair shows the defect alone cannot, since it is the same in A and B. The answer is that revising is necessary when the trouble remains. That is a fact about the problem. The question-first theorist can add that Ines will pose a new question if she still wants to know. Then the old inquiry is over and the new one starts from scratch, which makes the evidence gathered under the first relevant to the second only incidentally, and loses the fact that she is continuing the same work.

**Second, what distinguishes learning from failure from success.** If Ines in A is said to have failed informatively, we need something that separates her from an inquirer who watches for a year, finds nothing, and gives up. Neither answered her question, and both may have learned something. The difference is that Ines can stop and the other can do so only by quitting. Whatever the question-first theorist uses to mark the difference is a success condition that is not answering the question, and I submit that it will be the relief of the trouble.

**Third, retroactive verdicts.** Was the Michelson--Morley experiment a failed inquiry? If the question they asked has a false presupposition, then on the question-first picture they inquired into a defective question, which in Willard-Kyle's terms is a failed inquiry. That classification could not have been made in 1887, and it was made later partly on the strength of their own result. They produced a measured bound that later accounts of moving bodies had to accommodate, which is what Einstein's "unsuccessful attempts" refers to. A theory on which an experiment's status as a success flips when a later community retires its question, and flips partly because of the experiment, is a poor guide to what was good about it. On the problem view the experiment was a successful stage of an inquiry into how light propagates relative to moving bodies, because what it found was part of what relieved that problem. I use the ether as a case of a collective inquiry; the individual cases do the work of the argument, and the account of problems is meant to apply equally to groups that share one.

**Fourth, what the evaluative norms are for.** If the Knowledge Norm and its relatives are evaluative, as Palmira suggests, they should tell us which inquiries are good. They rate Ines in A, and the largest-prime inquirer, as having done something wrong or poorly. I deny it. A norm that rates the model cases of discovery as deficient is a poor guide to what is good about inquiring.

**What would show me wrong.** I take the following to count against the view.

1. A way to determine from the question alone, without appeal to the inquirer's problem, which of A and B is finished. If a theory of success for questions can distinguish them using only the question, its answers and their relation, my central claim fails. The enlarged answer space does not; I do not think any other will, but I would be shown wrong by one that did.
2. A convincing case of rational retirement where, after retirement, nothing in the inquirer's situation can be described as the trouble persisting or being relieved. Such a case would show that retirement can be rational without being governed by a problem.
3. Evidence that the premise of @sec-discovery is false for the cases that matter: that presupposition failures in open empirical inquiry are typically discovered by a separate prior check, by an inquiry into a different question that is not a way of pursuing the first. I have argued that the redescription dilemma makes this hard to state. But if inquirers do check presuppositions first and separately, the argument from discovery weakens, though the argument of @sec-success does not depend on it.
4. A principled account of problems on which my constraints against moving the goalposts fail, so that any inquiry can be reclassified as a success. I have given constraints; an example that evades all of them would defeat them.

# Closest prior work, and what this adds {#sec-prior}

*Permissibility.* The nearest work is on whether inquiry into questions that lack true answers can be permissible. Falbo argues that the norms forbidding such inquiry are overly restrictive and defends *Epistemic Improvement*: inquiry into Q is permissible only if it is not rational to be sure that by inquiring one will not improve epistemically upon Q, a view on which the value of inquiry goes beyond figuring out answers [@falbo2024]. This is the closest to my position on value. As far as I can see, though, her improvement is improvement upon Q, and her norm states a necessary condition on permissible inquiry, not a condition on success or a criterion for when an inquiry continues across a change of question. Palmira poses a puzzle about erotetic permissibility and defective inquiry and resolves it by distinguishing evaluative from prescriptive norms and appealing to zetetic trust [@palmira2025]. Hubacher Haerle's Success Norm ties rational inquiry to rational belief in success [@hubacherhaerle2025]. Rosa defends a norm against inquiry into pseudo-questions, including a reply to the objection that such inquiry can pay off [@rosa2025]. The thesis that inquiry into a defective question can be permissible, and even valuable, is theirs, not mine. I add three things. The first is that the issue is not only permission but success: the question-first assumption survives in the evaluative norms and the pro tanto defenses, and I argue against it with a minimal pair that no answer-space extension can handle. The second is the argument from discovery, which says the strong norms are idle or self-defeating as well as too strict, and which treats the redescription and conditional-question replies as dilemmas. The third is an account of what makes an inquiry the same inquiry across a change of question, and a condition of success that does not mention the question.

*Value, intention, answering.* Khalifa and Millson hold that only true answers to relevant questions are of fundamental epistemic value, with relevance fixed by the inquirer's interests, role and background assumptions [@khalifamillson2020]. That is nearby in making the questions that matter depend on the inquirer, but it is a thesis about value and keeps the question as the unit. D. Friedman's Intention Account makes inquiry a matter of an intention to answer a question "broadly construed" [@friedman2024]. If broad construal covers retiring the question, then my claim is partly absorbed into hers and the work is done by the construal. I take plan-theoretic structure to support my picture: an intention to answer Q is usually adopted in service of a further end, and when its object turns out to be defective rationality ordinarily requires revising the means and not dropping the end. That remark is mine, and I do not attribute it to her. Peacocke argues that a judgment whose content settles Q does not thereby answer Q in inquiry, and that saying what more is needed is an unsolved problem [@peacocke2026]. The question I raise is complementary: what it is for an inquiry to end well otherwise than by answering.

*Question-first norms.* Willard-Kyle is the closest to my target. He accepts that we sometimes revise our questions; he reports Ginzburg's view that the lower bound of resolution "floats" with the question's goal; and he requires only that an answer be conclusive enough, declining to settle what that comes to [@willardkyle2023, note to sec. 2.2]. These are points of contact, not agreement: the goal-sensitivity of how much of an answer is enough does not reach the question of when the question itself should be abandoned.

*Older ancestors.* Dewey's *Logic* [@dewey1938] is the obvious place to look for earlier versions of the thought that inquiry is organized by problems and not by questions. I have not worked through it and make no claim about what it contains.

*What is new.* Narrowly: the thesis that success is relative to a problem and not a question; the minimal pair; the discovery argument against norms forbidding inquiry into defective questions, including the replies from redescription and conditional questions; and the individuation condition. I do not claim that retiring questions is new, nor that inquiry into defective questions can be reasonable.

# Conclusion

When an inquirer learns that the question she has been pursuing has a false presupposition, one of two things is true. She has relieved what prompted it, and may rest; or she has not, and must go on, with another question. Which holds is not decided by the question or the defect. It is decided by the problem. The norms that forbid inquiry into defective questions do not capture this, and what they leave out is the part of inquiry in which defects come to light.
